newsitem.title: USA: UPS strike threat sends competitors, customers scrambling.
newsitem.headline: UPS strike threat sends competitors, customers scrambling.

text.p: The threat of a strike at United Parcel Service of America Inc. has competitors and customers of the world's largest package delivery company scrambling to cope with a potentially mammoth disruption.
UPS and the International Brotherhood of Teamsters were at loggerheads Thursday, hours after the union rejected what UPS called its final contract offer.

Unless a contract settlement is reached by midnight EDT, roughly two-thirds of UPS' domestic work force of 301,000 employees is set to walk off the job. That would bring a halt to all UPS domestic operations, where it controls about 80 percent of the parcel delivery market.

"UPS ships more than all the other carriers combined. There simply are not enough other carriers to pick up the slack," said Kathy Luhn, a spokesman with the National Industrial Transportation League, a Northern Virginia-based trade association. "This is going to have a tremendous effect."
Luhn said companies aren't the only ones affected.
She's been fielding phone calls from frantic individuals worried about the fate of personal items such as packages enroute to children away from home.

The growing reliance by businesses upon just-in-time delivery systems will exacerbate the effects of a Teamsters walkout, industry experts said. The strike could leave store shelves bereft of such items as electronics goods and pharmaceuticals.

As the strike deadline drew near, UPS customers were driven into a frantic search for alternative arrangements for their daily shipments of apparel, computers, documents and the millions of other personal and business parcels that fill UPS' fleet of 500 aircraft and 147,000 trucks.
Particularly vulnerable were mail order companies such as Lands' End Inc., which ship thousands of customer orders each day via UPS.

"We're obviously concerned, but we're explaining to customers as they place orders that there could be a delay in the delivery," Lands' End spokeswoman Anna Schryver said. UPS handles the "vast majority" of the 12 million orders Lands' End ships annually.
Companies such as LL Bean Co., which ships exclusively with UPS competitors, are the fortunate few. "We are sitting pretty," said a spokeswoman for Bean, which ships with Federal Express Corp..

Austin, Texas-based Dell Computer Corp. has alternative delivery plans in place that should allow it to survive a UPS strike "without a significant disruption to business," Dell spokesman T.R. Reid said.
UPS competitors were both eager to take advantage of the additional business and fearful of the chaotic effect a UPS work stoppage would have on their industry.

Given the sheer volume of the approximately 12 million parcel deliveries UPS handles on a daily basis, "the industry would be challenged to absorb even a portion of that," said Dave Funkalsrud, a spokesman for DHL Airways Inc.
Federal Express said it saw a "dramatic increase" in volume as its customers tried to avoid disruptions from a UPS strike. It said it would do its best to service the needs of existing customers.

But Federal Express, which was also coping with the crash of one of its jets Thursday morning at Newark International Airport, said it will not open new accounts until after the labour situation is resolved.

DHL, too, has seen a steadily rising volume of calls for service over the past three days, Funkalsrud said. It has gone so far as to alter the hold message on its telephone system to explain that the UPS situation could mean a longer-than-usual wait for customers wishing to talk to a service representative.

DHL will take on new business selectively, Funkalsrud said, with its priority being the handling of existing customers' needs. It said it had a contingency plan in place that involves the hiring of additional aircraft and adding temporary workers to handle added volume.

The U.S. Postal Service also had contingencies in place to accept more parcel traffic, spokesman Mark Saunders said. But the first priority will be assuring that added volume does not interfere with the delivery of its daily load of 600 million pieces of regular mail.
"We really have not seen an increasing volume yet," Saunders said.
